Header:
Date: 2026-03-21

Attendees: Sophie Martinez (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Empire Head of DS), Aisha Khan (Empire Platform), Raj Patel (CTO)

Summary (auto): quick cost economics/discovery focused on hosted vs dedicated vs private options; customer is budget conscious, looking at ~50M tokens/month steady-state, wants clear per-token math, batching/caching levers and pilot timeline. Action items captured.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching, committed vs on-demand dedicated, VPC/private deployment cost drivers, SLA and security concerns.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Michael: yea, loud and clear, thanks Sophie.
[00:05] Aisha: yep good here.
[00:07] Sophie: great quick intro, i'm Sophie Martinez, AE at Redwood, with Jordan our SE. we do a short cost econ discovery to understand volume, SLA, and which deployment mode makes sense - hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, or private in their VPC.
[00:20] Jordan: hey all, i'll mostly handle the infra/throughput questions so feel free to jump in if you want deeper perf numbers.
[00:27] Raj: cool, high level we want to replace some of our inference running on open-hosted endpoints and some homegrown serving. main ask is: can you give us per-token cost comparables and what levers we can pull to hit our cost target of around $0.0005 per token equivalent?
[00:42] Sophie: got it, that's the north star. before we jump into numbers, quick context - michael, can you confirm current volume and pattern?
[00:49] Michael: sure, we're at roughly 50 million tokens a month now, spikes during hours, about 1.2k RPS at peak across many small requests, average sequence length 120 tokens, tail going to 800 tokens occasionally. our batchable traffic is about 60%, rest is low-latency chat.
[01:08] Jordan: nice, that distribution helps. batching will matter a ton, also prefix caching for repeated context - our KV cache can shave a lot off for multi-step chat.
[01:16] Aisha: quick q, are you talking about Redwood hosted or our dedicated pods? like what's the switch?
[01:22] Sophie: both — we offer hosted with pay-as-you-go per-token rates, dedicated reserved capacity with committed monthly spend (lower unit cost), and private (VPC/on-prem) which adds infra overhead but gives data residency and direct network control. the key is to model token unit economics across those.
[01:36] Michael: can you walk through the math quickly - what is included in per-token? is it compute only or storage/kv cache costs extra?
[01:43] Jordan: good point. our per-token pricing for hosted includes the compute cost and service overhead, but persistent storage like long-term KV or additional retention is an add-on. for dedicated, you'd pay committed monthly for GPU pools plus service fee; caching/prefix hits effectively reduce tokens billed because we do prefix/KV reuse and we also offer local model variants that are cheaper per-token.
[02:03] Raj: when you say cheaper per-token with models, you mean quantized variants or smaller model families?
[02:07] Jordan: both - we provide curated model variants; for example a quantized 8-bit variant reduces compute time and memory, so throughput goes up and unit cost drops. also you can route low-latency traffic to a smaller but faster model.
[02:17] Michael: what's a realistic hosted number for 50M tokens? ballpark.
[02:20] Sophie: for hosted, with our current list prices and assuming moderate batching and 60% cacheable prefixes, rough ballpark is $0.0009 - $0.0012 per token. with brokerage (committed discount) or dedicated you can get down to $0.00045 - $0.0006 depending on GPU type and utilization.
[02:39] Michael: ok that aligns with internal estimates, their target 0.0005 looks doable if we commit. what are the commit levels needed for that?
[02:45] Sophie: typically you need a monthly committed reservation that covers most of steady-state. for 50M tokens a month — if you can commit to 80% of that we can structure a dedicated plan that hits around the $0.0005 range. Jordan can walk through GPU sizing.
[02:57] Jordan: right, for your seq length and 1.2k peak RPS, a couple of options: A100 80GB pools tuned for latency give the best latency SLAs but cost more; H100 or next-gen Ampere maybe cheaper per-token at high batch sizes. for cost-first, we recommend batching aggressively + a mix of quantized models on cheaper GPUs. I'll sketch a sizing: for 50M tokens with your mix, you'd need roughly 6-8 GPUs dedicated to hit throughput without adding too much latency, if you target 95th percentile latency under 300ms you might need more specialized infra.
[03:30] Aisha: question, how does prefix/KV cache reduce billing? like is Redwood billing fewer tokens or do you still bill generated tokens?
[03:36] Jordan: good question — for cache hits we can avoid re-decoding prefix tokens on the GPU and route to a lightweight path; billing semantics: for hosted we bill based on inference tokens consumed, but if a request hits the KV cache we only bill for the new tokens generated (not the cached prefix), so effective tokens billed drop. in dedicated/private modes you pay for the infra but your per-unit compute cost falls.
[04:00] Michael: there's often confusion around on-demand burst vs committed - can we burst above reserved? how are bursts priced?
[04:05] Sophie: yes, we support burst capacity on dedicated — you get baseline committed throughput and can burst into an on-demand pool at a higher unit price. the burst incurs on-demand unit pricing which is similar to hosted rates.
[04:15] Raj: security/compliance question — if we go dedicated in our VPC, do you still have access to logs? we need SOC2 plus KMS for keys, and audit logs for model access.
[04:24] Jordan: for Private/VPC deployments, control plane is customer-managed optionally; we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and can route logs to your SIEM. we offer SOC2 docs; i'll attach the security brief. note transcription: sometimes our docs show V-P-C spelled out but it's VPC.
[04:40] Aisha: are there other hidden costs — egress, storage, model updates?
[04:44] Sophie: egress for hosted is standard cloud egress, for dedicated it's typically included up to a threshold, but large model snapshot storage and long-term feature store are add-ons. model updates and version pinning have no additional per-token cost but large model transfers (pulling new weights) may incur one-time transfer charges.
[05:02] Michael: can you show an example cost table?
[05:05] Sophie: sure i have a quick example, i'll read it out: Hosted on-demand: $0.0010/token (base) at your mix -> 50M tokens = $50,000/month. With 60% cache/prefix hits effective billed tokens drop to ~20M generated tokens, net bill 20M *1.0e-3 = $20k. Dedicated committed: commit $30k/month for reserved GPUs + service fee -> effective unit around $0.0005 -> net $25k. those are simplified.
[05:34] Michael: wait the hosted math — you're assuming cache reduces billed tokens to 20M not 30M? can you clarify?
[05:39] Jordan: sorry, slip — baseline 50M tokens, 60% of tokens are prefix/cached so only 40% are billed as new tokens, so 50M * 0.4 = 20M. yes that was the calc.
[05:51] Raj: ok gotcha. for model accuracy we can't always route to the smaller model; what's the quality tradeoff?
[05:56] Jordan: we'll help you run evals on your prompts. sometimes smaller models or quantized variants are fine for reranking or summarization, but for long-form generation you may need the larger family. we can gate by route or by confidence thresholds.
[06:10] Aisha: latency SLOs are also tricky, our product needs <200ms p50 for chat. how realistic is that?
[06:15] Jordan: on dedicated low-latency GPUs and with batch windows tuned to be small, p50 under 200ms is achievable for 120 token sequences. the tradeoff is throughput and cost. for mixed workloads we recommend two routes: low-latency pool (higher cost per token) and a high-throughput pool (cheaper) for async jobs.
[06:33] Michael: how do we estimate the break-even point between hosted and dedicated? is there a simple formula?
[06:38] Sophie: a simple approach: compute monthly hosted bill at your observed effective billed tokens (apply cache/batching discounts), compare vs committed monthly cost including GPU lease + service fees. if committed < hosted by X% then dedicated wins. we can run a scenario model — i'll send a spreadsheet that takes your inputs.
[06:53] Raj: can you include different GPU classes and utilization in that sheet? we want to see H100 vs A100 vs cheaper Ampere options.
[06:59] Jordan: yes, i'll include model throughput per GPU, utilization assumptions, and amortized infra costs. note that quantization changes the throughput and memory which changes GPU choice.
[07:12] Michael: random question — are tokenization differences across models a cost factor? some models tokenize differently which impacts token counts and cost.
[07:18] Jordan: absolutely, tokenizer differences can affect token count by +/- 10-20% depending on model. we'll normalize to your target model family in the sheet.
[07:26] Aisha: what about batching latency impact — if you batch more you lower cost but increase tail latency. do you have auto-batching policies?
[07:33] Jordan: yes we have adaptive batching that targets latency SLOs; you can set a max batch window and we can prefer smaller batches for low-latency routes. also continuous batching works better in dedicated because utilization is higher.
[07:46] Sophie: to go back to pricing levers, they are: 1) choose deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private), 2) model family/quantization, 3) batching window and router policies, 4) prefix/KV cache hit rate, 5) committed utilization level.
[07:58] Michael: can you run a sensitivity for us? like if cache hits are only 30% vs 60% what's the impact?
[08:03] Jordan: yes, in the sheet i'll include scenarios: 30/45/60% cache hit and 40/60/80% committed utilization. that shows the delta clearly.
[08:12] Raj: who are some customers running similar economics? examples?
[08:15] Sophie: a number of fintechs and conversational ai companies — we have references but i'll get permission to share specific names. high level: customers moving from hosted to dedicated usually hit 30-60% unit cost reductions with commitments + batching.
[08:29] Michael: what's the onboarding pilot look like? can we start hosted and move to dedicated?
[08:33] Sophie: yes, common pattern is start hosted, instrument with our tracing and cost dashboards, then once usage is stable we model committed capacity and plan a migration. timeline is typically 4-8 weeks for a pilot to production depending on access to traces and infra signoff.
[08:48] Aisha: do we need any special networking for private? we have strict VPC peering rules.
[08:52] Jordan: for private we do either customer-managed control plane or an on-prem package; network-wise we support VPC peering, private link, and can run behind the customer's firewall with certs. there are additional infra setup charges for private deployments.
[09:07] Michael: can you put expected engineering effort on the migration? like how many person-weeks?
[09:12] Sophie: rough estimate: hosted instrumentation -> 1-2 engineer-weeks; dedicated sizing + infra set up 2-4 weeks; private/VPC more like 4-6 weeks with security review. will vary.
[09:25] Raj: any concerns about multi-region latencies if we keep hosted? we're in NA and EU.
[09:29] Jordan: hosted is multi-region, we can route traffic by policy; dedicated can be regional too but if you need global low-latency you may need more pools, which increases committed costs. we'll model that.
[09:43] Michael: what about model fallback - if a dedicated pool is saturated does Redwood fall back to hosted?
[09:49] Sophie: yes, we can set routing policies with automatic fallback to hosted or a cheaper model variant. that's part of resiliency and helps avoid dropped requests.
[09:57] Aisha: for the spike patterns we have, bursting seems important. can you give example pricing for burst traffic?
[10:02] Jordan: bursting is priced at on-demand hosted rates typically ~1.5x base hosted per-token. we'll include in scenario.
[10:11] Michael: anything else materially that increases cost? cold start model loads?
[10:15] Jordan: model snapshot pull is one-time; if you spin up new instances frequently that can add infra transient costs; but under dedicated steady state that's amortized. plus SLO-driven scaling can add cost if you always maintain headroom.
[10:28] Sophie: ok want to switch to concrete next steps - we need token traces and peak patterns and we'll send the spreadsheet.
[10:34] Michael: yea we'll share a week's traces and our prompt set.
[10:37] Raj: include sample prompt list so you can run evals.
[10:40] Sophie: perfect. Jordan, i'll have you assemble the sizing and security attachments.
[10:45] Jordan: will do.
[10:47] Michael: one last thing - do you have examples where customers got to $0.0004?
[10:51] Sophie: we've seen mid-size customers with high utilization and aggressive batching + quantization get below $0.0004 per effective token but that requires high commitment and being able to route a large percent of traffic to optimized paths. i'll include a caveat in the spreadsheet.
[11:05] Aisha: ok thanks all.
[11:07] Sophie: thanks we'll follow up with docs and scheduled sizing call.
